Volume 15 · Chapter 01

Public economics and taxation

Advanced Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v05, v06, v12, v13

By the endAnalyze tax and spending decisions with efficiency and distribution in view.

Capability and prerequisites

Analyze who bears a tax, what behavior it changes, how public revenue is used, and which ethical weights support a recommendation. Derive an implementable tax or insurance allocation instead of announcing an unconstrained social optimum. Prerequisites are the accepted microeconomics, macroeconomics, econometrics and graduate theory volumes: constrained choice, equilibrium, concavity, incentive compatibility and causal identification. All numerical economies below are original synthetic examples. They describe no jurisdiction's current tax law.

The budget committee's missing comparison

A government proposes a consumption tax to fund a common service and insurance against lost income. One memorandum counts the tax bill as a social loss. Another counts the same revenue as a free social benefit. A third assigns the entire burden to the business legally remitting the tax. None has yet specified the relevant counterfactual. Tax receipts move purchasing power; producing the service uses resources; changed work, trade, reporting and insurance behavior can change the available resources. Each belongs in a different equation.

Public economics combines positive analysis—equilibrium responses and causal evidence—with normative analysis—whose welfare matters and how. The distinction does not make distribution optional. It makes the value judgment explicit. A policy may increase a weighted objective while making someone worse off; it may be potentially compensating without actually paying compensation; and it may satisfy a budget while violating private incentives.

Use a common accounting unit before adding benefits and costs. A unit tax t is goods per transaction; a proportional tax τ is dimensionless; q is a physical quantity; p is goods per unit; tax revenue is tq. A welfare weight g multiplies a person's utility or marginal money value under a specified normalization. Probability p in the insurance section is separately introduced and never a market price. Population masses sum to one in the income-tax model; the public-good example instead has two whole people. These normalizations matter for budgets.

1. Incidence is an equilibrium derivative

Let competitive demand be D(pᶜ), supply S(pᵖ), and a fully enforced unit tax impose pᶜ=pᵖ+t. Consumers choose at the gross price and producers at the net price. At an interior equilibrium S(pᵖ)=D(pᵖ+t), assume differentiability, S′≥0, D′≤0 and S′−D′>0. Implicit differentiation gives

dpᵖ/dt=D′/(S′−D′),   dpᶜ/dt=S′/(S′−D′),   dq/dt=S′D′/(S′−D′).

The derivatives sum to a one-unit wedge and quantity weakly falls. The legal remitter is absent: writing the same wedge on the buyer's or seller's return leaves the equilibrium unchanged under these assumptions. Different enforcement, salience, credit constraints or market power can invalidate that equivalence. At a zero-tax baseline, common price p and quantity q convert the buyer share into εS/(εS+|εD|). At an existing tax, gross and net prices differ, so substituting unadjusted elasticities into the zero-wedge expression is generally wrong. Zero demand responsiveness places the price burden on consumers; zero supply responsiveness places it on producers. A vertical curve is best handled as a quantity constraint or an appropriate limit, not by differentiating a nonexistent price function.

Under quasilinear preferences, no other distortions or externalities, and competitive marginal cost, total real surplus at quantity q is the integral of inverse demand minus inverse supply. Revenue is a transfer within that total if it is returned without resource loss. A tax removes mutually beneficial marginal trades; the lost area is its excess burden. With nonlinear schedules a triangle is a local approximation; with linear schedules it is exact. If pollution, monopoly, another tax or an omitted market already creates a wedge, the efficient comparison and the sign of a small reform's welfare effect can change. These scope distinctions connect to the incidence methods in Saez's incidence lecture; the following calculations are independently constructed.

Worked case 1 — prices, receipts and lost trades

Suppose (demand intercept,demand slope,supply slope,t)=(120,2,3,10), so D=120−2pᶜ and S=3pᵖ. Prices and quantities are nonnegative; we consider 0≤t≤60. Clearing gives pᵖ=24−2t/5, pᶜ=24+3t/5 and q=72−6t/5. At t=10, (pᵖ,pᶜ,q,revenue)=(20,30,60,600). Consumers pay six more per remaining unit and producers receive four less; those changes are not the same as total welfare losses, because quantities also move.

Inverse demand is60−q/2 and inverse supply q/3. Before tax, consumer surplus is(1/2)(60−24)72=1296 and producer surplus is(1/2)24·72=864. After tax they are900 and600; their losses396+264=660 equal revenue600 plus 60 in lost surplus. Direct integration over q∈[60,72] gives the same60. At t=20, q=48 and total excess burden is240. Raising the existing tax from10to20 therefore costs180 additional surplus, not the60 triangle calculated as if the initial tax were zero. The government's use of the receipts must now be evaluated separately; neither confiscating nor returning goods creates the vanished trades.

2. Optimal means optimal over an explicit feasible policy class

A government cannot generally choose each person's consumption and effort as though ability, effort and need were observable and contractible. A tax schedule T(z) conditions on observed earnings z. Net consumption is z−T(z), the marginal retention rate is1−T′(z), and the average tax rate T(z)/z is a different object. Participation compares the complete utility of working and not working, including fixed costs and T(0); an intensive-margin derivative does not settle it. Income effects, migration, evasion and reclassification must be included if they are feasible responses.

Start with a transparent restricted policy class to see exactly where welfare weights enter. There is a continuum of workers with productivity aᵢ>0 and masses μᵢ. Each supplies l≥0 at constant wage aᵢ and has utility c−l²/2. Competitive constant-returns production converts effective labor aᵢl into the consumption good, so wages exhaust output. A linear tax τ∈[0,1] funds a uniform transfer B: c=(1−τ)aᵢl+B. Individuals are atomistic and take B as given. Strict concavity gives lᵢ=(1−τ)aᵢ, including zero at τ=1. Define A=Σμᵢaᵢ². Balanced revenue gives B=τ(1−τ)A, and aggregate consumption equals aggregate output(1−τ)A.

Take fixed nonnegative social weights gᵢ with Σμᵢgᵢ=1 and define H=Σμᵢgᵢaᵢ². Indirect utility is Vᵢ=(1/2)(1−τ)²aᵢ²+B, hence

W(τ)=(H/2)(1−τ)²+Aτ(1−τ),   W(τ)−W(0)=(A−H)τ−(A−H/2)τ².

If 0<H<A, the quadratic is strictly concave and its unique maximum is τ*=(A−H)/(2A−H), between zero and one half. If H≥A, no positive tax improves W: when H≤2A both displayed terms are nonpositive; when H>2A, use τ²≤τ to bound the difference by−Hτ/2. Thus τ*=0. These are global statements on the specified policy interval. The revenue maximum is τ=1/2 regardless of the weights, and is generally a different objective. Quasilinearity rules out income effects; fixed productivities rule out wage incidence; restricting government to linear taxes rules out nonlinear improvements. Do not present this optimum as an unrestricted tax theorem. Saez's optimal-tax lecture supplies the broader method context of earnings incentives, revenue responses and distributional objectives; this exact two-type construction and its proof are original.

Worked case 2 — changing ethical weights changes the recommendation

Let (μL,μH,aL,aH,gL,gH)=(1/2,1/2,1,3,3/2,1/2). Then A=5,H=3, so (τ*,B*)=(2/7,50/49). Labor is(5/7,15/7), earnings(5/7,45/7), consumption(75/49,275/49), and utilities(125/98,325/98). Weighted welfare is 25/14, compared with3/2at zero tax. Mean consumption is25/7, exactly mean output. Net taxes differ by type but sum to zero after transfers.

At τ=1/2 revenue/transfer is5/4, greater than50/49, while weighted welfare is13/8, less than25/14. Maximizing receipts is not maximizing this welfare objective. With equal weights gL=gH=1, H=A and the optimum is zero: equal marginal utility of goods and equal ethical weights leave no redistributive gain in this quasilinear model. That conclusion would change under concave utility of consumption or other social weights. Observing labor responses identifies neither the chosen weights nor the morally appropriate objective.

Worked case 3 — a balanced allocation can fail self-selection

Now use two equally numerous types with abilities (1,2). Earnings z require effort z/a, and utility is c−z²/(2a²). The government can offer only a two-item earnings/consumption menu, no other earnings options; this is a direct-menu illustration, not a complete nonlinear schedule on every real earnings level. It wants earnings (1,2) and no public spending. Giving both types consumption3/2 balances average output and consumption, but a high type prefers the low menu: utility11/8instead of1. Balance alone did not implement the assigned labor.

For both selections to be weakly optimal, the consumption difference d=cH−cL must satisfy (zH²−zL²)/(2aH²)≤d≤(zH²−zL²)/(2aL²), here3/8≤d≤3/2. The lower inequality prevents the high type imitating the low; the upper prevents the low type imitating the high. With cL+cH=3 and minimum high-type rent, choose (21/16,27/16). Low utility is13/16and high utility19/16; the high type's low-menu utility is also19/16. We explicitly assign truthful selection at indifference. For strict high-type selection raise d slightly above3/8, reducing cL and increasing cH by equal amounts; remain below3/2. All resource accounts still close.

This proves implementability of the stated menu, not optimality among earnings targets or tax schedules. A full mechanism-design problem must jointly choose z,c, impose participation and every relevant report/deviation, and specify off-menu opportunities. It also needs ability distribution and welfare weights. The example explains why a high consumption allocation can include an information rent without treating that rent as a resource cost or an ethical entitlement.

3. Public goods require a common-quantity comparison

A pure public good is nonrival: another user's access does not reduce the physical amount available to the first. Nonexcludability concerns the technology or institution of restricting access. Neither property is synonymous with government ownership. Congestion can make a facility partly rival; a subscription can make access excludable; and tax-financed private goods remain private goods. Model the relevant margin rather than classifying everything a government buys as public.

With private consumptions cᵢ and a common quantity G, feasibility is Σcᵢ+C(G)≤Σwᵢ. For differentiable increasing utilities Uᵢ(cᵢ,G), positive welfare weights and an interior efficient allocation, the planner's FOCs imply λᵢUᵢc=η for each i and ΣλᵢUᵢG=ηC′. Dividing yields Σ(UᵢG/Uᵢc)=C′: sum marginal willingness to pay for the same extra unit. Distribution affects these marginal rates through consumption; it has not disappeared. Concavity of utilities and convexity of resource cost can make supporting conditions sufficient, while nonconvex projects require a global comparison. The public-goods lecture identifies this common-quantity principle and the private-contribution problem; our funding and equilibrium example follows directly from its own primitives.

Worked case 4 — an efficient service still needs an acceptable bill

Two people each own10goods and value a nonrival service G=g₁+g₂. Their utilities are10−gᵢ+aᵢlog(1+G), with (a1,a2,cost per unit)=(2,1,1). Contributions are nonnegative and cannot exceed wealth. Marginal utility in own contribution is−1+aᵢ/(1+G), strictly decreasing. Best response is max{aᵢ−1−gⱼ,0}, subject to the wealth cap; that cap never binds here. Person2 never contributes positively, while person1 gives1. Thus the unique Nash allocation is (g1,g2,G)=(1,0,1).

Total surplus is20−G+3log(1+G), strictly concave, with derivative−1+3/(1+G). Its unique global optimum is 2. Relative to voluntary provision the aggregate utility gain is−1+3log(3/2)>0. Financing G=2with bills(17/10,3/10) gives individual gains (0.110930216216,0.105465108108); both are positive and bills sum to real cost2. A different split can make one person lose, despite the same efficient quantity. Actual compensation matters.

These payments assume enforceable lump-sum contributions and known values. If taxes distort earnings, collection consumes resources, values are privately reported or political consent binds, the feasible problem changes. Personalized marginal public-good prices can support a chosen efficient quantity under suitable budgets, but declaring such prices does not elicit truthful values. The mechanism-design constraints studied earlier remain relevant.

4. Social insurance: smooth consumption and preserve the required incentives

Insurance transfers goods across states before the state is known; redistribution across known types is a different comparison, although a single institution can do both. For an exogenous loss probability p, initial wealth w, loss L and benefit b, an actuarially balanced contract charges premium pb. Consumption is cG=w−pb without loss and cB=w−L+(1−p)b with loss. If utility is strictly concave and p∈(0,1), expected consumption w−pL is independent of b. Jensen's inequality makes full insurance b=L uniquely optimal over 0≤b≤L. The result requires positive consumption, no loading, the stated risk and feasible pooling.

When prevention changes the loss probability and is unobserved, the insured person chooses effort taking the offered premium and benefit fixed. The premium cannot be recomputed after a unilateral hidden deviation. Adverse selection instead concerns privately known risk types before the contract. Neither phenomenon is a moral judgment about a claimant. Verification costs, take-up, administrative errors and correlated aggregate losses also affect feasible insurance. Saez's insurance introduction provides the risk-pooling and hidden-action context; the next example explicitly solves the incentive and funding constraints instead of assuming partial coverage is always best.

Worked case 5 — solve both effort regimes before comparing insurance

Consider a unit continuum with independent idiosyncratic risks and deterministic cross-sectional loss frequencies, no aggregate risk. Everyone starts with w=10and can lose L=6. Effort e∈{0,1} changes loss probability from1/2to1/4and costs k=log(3/2)/4utility, not goods. Preferences are expected log consumption minus ke. A mandatory uniform contract chooses benefit b∈[0,6] and a premium equal to its equilibrium expected payment. There is no loading, reserve cost, type heterogeneity or outside option constraint. These assumptions delimit the comparison. The primitives are (w,L,p0,p1)=(10,6,1/2,1/4).

Under a proposed effort equilibrium, premium is b/4, so cG=10−b/4,cB=4+3b/4. Holding that premium fixed, effort improves utility by(1/4)log(cG/cB)−k. Therefore effort is incentive compatible exactly when cG/cB≥3/2, equivalently b≤32/11. At equality select effort; without this tie convention the limiting optimum requires a strict-margin adjustment. Expected log utility under effort has derivative(3/16)(1/cB−1/cG)>0 for b<6. Consequently its best incentive-compatible benefit is (b,premium,cG,cB)=(32/11,8/11,102/11,68/11). The derivative and compact interval prove global optimality within this regime.

Under no effort, actuarial premium is b/2and mean consumption is7. Jensen bounds its utility by log7, attained at full insurance b=6. At full coverage effort would only incur its cost, so no effort is indeed optimal; this contract is implementable. The effort contract's utility simplifies to log[(68/11)√(3/2)], which exceeds log7 because (68/11)²(3/2)>49. Its welfare advantage is 0.078434837377. Every deterministic uniform contract must induce one of the two effort regimes; their best feasible values have been compared. Mixed effort, menus, risk-type screening and randomized contracts are outside this policy class.

Under effort the average loss is3/2, and average consumption is17/2. Premium8/11equals(1/4)(32/11), while the insurance payment is a transfer, not a reversal of the physical loss. Higher mean goods than under no effort must be compared with effort's utility cost and residual risk. In a finite population premiums balanced in expectation would require capital, reserves or contingent assessments to meet realized claims; the continuum pooling assumption is doing work here. This is an ex ante welfare result within the specified group, not an assertion that all realized claimants gain.

5. Identify the behavioral margin before using it in welfare analysis

An earnings response can combine hours, participation, human-capital investment, migration, timing and reporting. A change in taxable income is a fiscal base change; it is not automatically a loss of real output. In a reduced-form tax experiment, first define the treatment unit, pre-reform assignment, exposure, outcome, counterfactual and horizon. A difference in differences needs untreated trends and no relevant interference under the target estimand. A threshold design needs continuity of counterfactual outcomes and no decisive sorting; a tax threshold can coincide with another benefit threshold. A simulated tax instrument based on predetermined characteristics still needs exclusion and a credible first stage. These requirements use the identification tools of Volume12.

A local sufficient-statistic calculation is useful only when its structural envelope and fiscal externalities fit the actual reform. If a base falls because income moves into another taxed category, the destination government's receipts belong in the budget. If resources are spent concealing income, those costs differ from transfers between accounts. Measuring a reduced-form elasticity without the enforcement regime, tax base or time horizon leaves its policy transportability unresolved. Saez's tax lecture distinguishes real and reporting responses; it does not establish that one elasticity applies in every institutional setting.

Worked case 6 — an identified base change is not a complete policy verdict

A synthetic treatment group has mean taxable income100before and90after a reform. An untreated comparison goes from80to84. The treatment marginal rate rises from1/5to3/10. Maintain parallel untreated trends in levels, stable composition and no spillovers. Inputs are (Tpre,Tpost,Cpre,Cpost,old rate,new rate)=(100,90,80,84,1/5,3/10). The counterfactual treated mean is104, so the effect is−14. Treating this change as a uniform proportional response for this illustrative group gives arc elasticity log(90/104)/log[(7/10)/(4/5)]=1.082750849590. The log calculation uses the estimated counterfactual, not the old mean100. A ratio of aggregate means need not equal an average individual elasticity.

Counterfactual tax receipts are(1/5)104=104/5; reform receipts are27. The gain 31/5 decomposes into mechanical(1/10)104=52/5plus behavioral(3/10)(−14)=−21/5. Comparing27with the previous20instead would mix policy and untreated growth. If an independently valid real-output measure falls only4and the remaining10is income relabeling, the full fourteen-unit base response cannot be called fourteen goods of lost production. The destination tax treatment and actual avoidance costs are still needed.

This four-mean table supplies neither standard errors nor a credible design by itself; its identifying assumptions were imposed. Preserve microdata provenance, cluster structure, selection and attrition rules, pre-reform diagnostics, concurrent policies and a prespecified horizon. Welfare additionally needs affected people's money-metric values, chosen weights, revenue use, enforcement costs and general-equilibrium effects. A positive revenue estimate does not settle those questions.

6. Turn a recommendation into a testable institution

Write a policy comparison in five linked statements. Specify the feasible rule and legal or administrative authority; enumerate whose behavior changes and whose resources fund it; state the objective and distributional weights; identify the evidence needed for the uncertain response; and define monitoring, an appeals mechanism and a revision condition. These are not extra benefits to add mechanically to a welfare sum. They are constraints and information requirements of the allocation.

For a proposed earnings tax, record the base, filing unit, timing, interaction with transfers, withholding and enforcement costs. For a public service, record access and congestion, procurement and maintenance, funding and displaced private provision. For insurance, record verifiable eligibility, benefit timing, contribution incidence, reserves for aggregate risk and the treatment of denied claims. A model with costless enforcement cannot determine a real implementation budget. A model with private information cannot assume a perfect registry simply to reach its first best.

A useful distribution table separates gross benefits, taxes, price changes and behavioral costs by affected group. Do not add a transfer paid by one group to the same transfer received by another as net resources. Report both weighted welfare and each group's change. Test the conclusion under defensible alternative weights and parameter ranges. A proposal that survives no plausible sensitivity case should not be described as robust; a proposal that survives some cases but not others has an identifiable decision condition.

Exercises

Use exact values where possible. Every model is the stated synthetic economy. For open questions, defend assumptions and a falsifiable comparison; no political position is prescribed.

  1. In case1 set t=5. Derive both prices, quantity, receipts and excess burden. Show how consumer and producer surplus losses divide into revenue and lost trades.
  2. A monopolist faces inverse demand100−2q, constant marginal cost20and unit tax10. Find the global quantity and price before/after tax. Compare consumer price pass-through with a competitive constant-cost supplier. Explain why case1's zero-distortion welfare triangle cannot be transplanted unchanged.
  3. In case2 change welfare weights to(gL,gH)=(7/4,1/4), retaining all economic primitives. Find the global optimal rate, transfer and weighted welfare. Explain why this is an ethical sensitivity analysis rather than a newly estimated behavioral response.
  4. In case3 change assigned earnings to(zL,zH)=(1,3), keeping abilities(1,2)and equal masses. Derive the complete interval for cH−cL, and the balanced minimum-rent menu and both utilities. State the tie and policy-space limitations.
  5. In case4 raise the real cost per unit of G to2. Contributions purchase giunits at cost2gi. Solve every private best response and the Nash total; derive the efficient total and total resource cost. Does a zero individual contribution prove zero social value?
  6. Return to case4's unit cost. An outside authority reimburses fractionσof each contribution and finances the reimbursement by equal lump-sum taxes on the two people. Chooseσso the private-contribution equilibrium provides efficient G=2. Verify contributions, tax bills, both final payments and both utility gains from the original voluntary allocation. Treat taxes as fixed privately.
  7. In case5 set effort cost to zero. Compare full-coverage contracts with premiums based on each possible effort regime. Explain exactly how the tie convention matters for implementing the high-effort, fully insured allocation.
  8. Instead set effort cost k=log2/4. Solve the best high-effort contract and compare it with the best no-effort contract. Does the presence of hidden effort logically imply the optimum must provide partial insurance?
  9. In case6 suppose a valid uncertainty procedure gives a treatment-effect interval[−20,−8], holding the counterfactual mean104fixed for this sensitivity calculation. Derive the implied reform-receipt and net-revenue intervals. Explain why positive revenue throughout is insufficient for a welfare recommendation and why this interval need not be a valid joint confidence region.
  10. A researcher compares people immediately above/below an earnings threshold after a tax change and calls the observed outcome gap causal. Give a defensible design revision covering assignment, manipulation, concurrent policies, outcome timing and fiscal interpretation. State one observed failure that would stop the claimed identification.
  11. A small reform gives a low-income group10goods, takes10from a high-income group and uses2additional goods of collection resources paid by that high-income group. Assume each group's local marginal utility of goods is one and ethical weights are3/2and1/2. Compute weighted welfare and unweighted net resources. Explain why this is neither a Pareto improvement nor a full large-reform welfare theorem.
  12. The committee wants to add the gains from cases2,4and5and call their sum the benefit of one national program. Diagnose the problem, then specify a minimal joint budget/model and evidence plan that could support a valid combined comparison. Include one prespecified implementation stop or revision rule.
Full solutions and evaluation criteria
  1. Clearing gives (pᵖ,pᶜ,q,revenue,DWL)=(22,27,66,330,15). Consumer surplus is(1/2)33·66=1089, loss207; producer surplus is(1/2)22·66=726, loss138. Total345equals330+15. Inverse-demand minus inverse-supply integration over[66,72]proves the fifteen-unit loss; the formulas hold within positive trade. Full credit requires the wedge, equilibrium and complete reconciliation, not revenue alone.
  2. Profit is(100−2q−20−t)qon0≤q≤50. It is strictly concave with derivative80−t−4q. Thus at t=0quantity20price60; at t=10quantity35/2price65, net received55. (q0,p0,q1,p1,pass-through)=(20,60,35/2,65,1/2). Marginal-cost competition instead pins net price20and makes gross price rise by the full ten. The monopolist already restricts trade below efficient q=40; the tax removes additional trades whose marginal benefit minus real cost starts positive even at the old monopoly quantity. Use inverse demand minus real marginal cost,80−2q, rather than marginal profit80−4q. Its integral over[35/2,20] is 425/4. This explicit correction illustrates why the chosen objective matters. Tax revenue175is transferred; it does not cancel the real lost-trade area. Full credit requires the correct surplus integrand and the global concavity/domain argument.
  3. A=5and H=(1/2)[(7/4)1+(1/4)9]=2. The strictly concave quadratic gives (τ,B,W)=(3/8,75/64,25/16). Labor is(5/8,15/8),and weighted utility is(1−τ)²+5τ(1−τ)=25/64+75/64. We changed only the ethical weights, not preferences, wages or feasible taxes; the labor-response functions were held fixed. The comparison therefore reports the dependence of a recommendation on stated values.
  4. Self-selection gives(9−1)/8≤d≤(9−1)/2,so1≤d≤4. Balance cL+cH=4and d=1give (cL,cH,UL,UH)=(3/2,5/2,1,11/8). The high type's low-item utility is3/2−1/8=11/8,so truthful selection is weak; make d>1slightly for strict high-type selection. Low types prefer their item because1>5/2−9/2. Consumption positivity further restricts d<4if strict positivity is imposed on this balanced menu; d=4would leave cL=0,which is allowed by linear consumption utility only if the consumption domain includes zero. This is implementability for the stated two-item menu, not proof the earnings target is socially optimal or that unspecified off-menu earnings cannot attract deviations.
  5. Best response is max{ai/2−1−gj,0}. Person1's derivative is zero only at totalG=0and negative above; person2's is negative even at zero. Strict concavity makes both choose zero, giving the unique Nash total0. The planner derivative is−2+3/(1+G),so (G_Nash,G_opt,cost)=(0,1/2,1). At zero, combined willingness to pay is3>2although neither person privately wants a positive contribution. Private incentives and joint benefits differ.
  6. An atomistic response to a fixed lump-sum tax uses private marginal cost1−σ. To get G=2with only the higher-value person contributing, require2/(1−σ)−1=2,soσ=1/3. At G=2the low type's marginal benefit1/3is below private cost2/3,so it contributes zero. Reimbursement is2/3, financed by taxes1/3each. Final total payments are (5/3,1/3),summing to real cost2. Gains relative to(g1,g2)=(1,0)are−2/3+2log(3/2)and−1/3+log(3/2),both positive, approximately (0.144263549550,0.072131774775). Privately endogenous tax bills or distortionary financing would alter these best responses.
  7. At zero effort cost and full benefit6, an effort-based premium3/2gives cG=cB=17/2. Under the specified effort-at-indifference convention, high effort is optimal and receipts/payments balance. A no-effort premium3gives common consumption7. Thus (effort insured consumption,no-effort insured consumption)=(17/2,7),and the first is better. Without the tie convention a person can choose no effort at the same fixed premium3/2, raising payouts above receipts; the intended high-effort contract is not robust to that selection. A small strictly positive uninsured loss can restore a strict effort advantage when cost is zero. Hidden effort alone does not logically forbid full coverage under an explicitly maintained selection rule.
  8. Effort requires cG/cB≥2,so10−b/4≥2(4+3b/4),or b≤8/7. Expected utility increases in bwithin this regime, giving (b,premium,cG,cB)=(8/7,2/7,68/7,34/7). Its net utility is log[(34/7)√2]. The no-effort optimum remains log7under full coverage, and(34/7)²·2=2312/49<49. Therefore no effort with full insurance wins globally within the two-regime deterministic uniform-contract class. The higher effort cost outweighs prevention's benefit after incentive constraints. This counterexample disproves a universal partial-insurance conclusion; it does not assess real insurance programs.
  9. Reform mean income lies in[84,96],so receipts lie in[126/5,144/5]. Subtract counterfactual104/5to obtain (net revenue lower,upper)=(22/5,8). Welfare still needs real versus reporting responses, distributional weights, funding use and collection costs. Holding the counterfactual fixed ignores its uncertainty and covariance with the treatment-effect estimate; transforming an interval this way is a conditional sensitivity calculation unless a joint statistical procedure justifies it.
  10. Define treatment using a predetermined running variable and the actual policy rule; post-reform earnings may itself respond to treatment. Establish the relevant continuity comparison, inspect density and predetermined covariates for sorting, and inventory benefits or administrative rules changing at the same cutoff. Freeze outcome dates and the local target population; report first-stage treatment take-up, bandwidth sensitivity and uncertainty appropriate to the design. Translate the outcome into taxable and real resources separately. A simultaneous benefit discontinuity with no design separating it from the tax would stop a tax-only causal claim; so would decisive sorting inconsistent with the maintained continuity argument. Full credit requires all five design elements and a concrete stopping condition, not the statement that a discontinuity is automatically exogenous.
  11. The low group gains10and the high group loses12. Weighted local welfare is(3/2)10−(1/2)12=9;unweighted real resources change by−2. The ten-good transfer cancels in aggregate resources, while collection consumes two. High-income welfare falls, so the reform is not Pareto improving. Constant local marginal values and fixed ethical weights justify this small-change calculation; for a large reform integrate changing marginal utilities, endogenous behavior and actual funding effects instead of extrapolating the linear number.
  12. The cases use different populations, production structures, risk assumptions and utility normalizations. Their reported gains are not commensurable national totals, and the same tax receipts or private resources could be counted more than once. Define one population with productivity, service values and loss risks, one dated goods constraint, labor/insurance/service choices, an explicit tax and benefit rule, and a common welfare objective. Derive private incentives under that combined rule before solving its budget; count administrative resources and risk reserves. Identify each behavioral response using a stated assignment and counterfactual, preserve data access/versions and assess how the estimates transport to the joint population. One revision rule is to pause expansion if audited eligibility errors exceed a prespecified tolerable bound or if observed reserve needs violate funded capacity; specify how that threshold is chosen before observing outcomes. Full credit requires accounting integration, incentives, ethical normalization, evidence and an actionable rule. A recommendation's sign may legitimately remain unresolved.

Teach-back

In three minutes explain how a tax can raise revenue, reduce unweighted surplus and raise weighted welfare simultaneously. Then explain why an allocation that balances the budget may still fail incentive compatibility. Use one explicit equation and identify the person financing each payment.

Teach-back answer guide

Use revenue tqas a transfer, the lost-trades area as an efficiency cost, and ΣgᵢΔVᵢas the distribution-sensitive objective. A net transfer toward a larger weight can outweigh a real cost under those weights while leaving a payer worse off. Then use case3: equal consumption balances output but makes the high type choose the low-earnings item. A complete explanation keeps normative weights, real resources and feasible deviations distinct.

Delayed retention

After a week, without notes: (1) derive the competitive buyer tax share from S(p)=D(p+t); (2) state the two self-selection inequalities for a two-type menu; (3) explain why a hidden-action deviation holds the premium fixed; (4) name one reason a taxable-income response differs from a real-output response.

Retention answer key

(1)Differentiate to get(S′−D′)p′=D′and buyer share1+p′=S′/(S′−D′), under the stated nonzero denominator and differentiability. (2)For aH>aL and zH≥zL, require(zH²−zL²)/(2aH²)≤cH−cL≤(zH²−zL²)/(2aL²), plus budget and participation where required. (3)The action is hidden and a unilateral individual cannot rewrite the offered contract; repricing it after the deviation removes the incentive problem being studied. (4)Income may move across tax categories or dates while production is unchanged; actual concealment costs or labor reductions require separate measurement.

Source scope and next step

The four linked Berkeley teaching documents were inspected on9October2026for the bounded methodological passages recorded with this chapter. They are further-reading routes, not sources for the synthetic numbers, policy recommendations or exercises. Their jurisdiction-specific illustrations and historical tax figures are not adopted as current law here. This chapter supplies original proofs within small explicit policy classes; it does not replace the full nonlinear taxation, general-equilibrium incidence or dynamic social-insurance literatures. Next, labor economics adds human capital, participation, discrimination and mobility, which can materially change the feasible responses to these policies.

Sources and further study

  • Emmanuel Saez, UC Berkeley Econ131 — Incidence and Efficiency Costs of Taxation — Competitive price wedge and bounded excess-burden context; original chapter directly derives its formulas.
  • Emmanuel Saez, UC Berkeley Econ131 — Optimal Labor Income Taxation — Income-tax method context; no imported current rates or unrestricted optimal-tax theorem.
  • Emmanuel Saez, UC Berkeley Econ131 — Public Goods — Public-good efficiency context; original quasilinear contribution/funding model.
  • Emmanuel Saez, UC Berkeley Econ131 — Social Insurance: Introduction — Insurance risk and incentive context; original two-effort global comparison explicitly avoids a universal partial-coverage claim.
